title: Zilch Commits £77m to Victoria HQ as European Expansion Accelerates
snippet: Zilch will take 33,160 sq ft at 40 Grosvenor Place on a 10-year lease, more than doubling capacity ahead of its planned Fjord The post Zilch Commits £77m to Victoria HQ as European Expansion Accelerates appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Zilch has signed a 10-year lease on a new London headquarters at 40 Grosvenor Place in Victoria, committing £77 million over the lease term and more than doubling its current office footprint. The buy-now-pay-later and payments platform will occupy floors four and five of the building, a 33,160 sq ft space the company says can accommodate more than 400 employees. Zilch expects to relocate from its current base at 111 Buckingham Palace Road in Spring 2027.

The investment manager for the building is PATRIZIA, represented by CBRE and Knight Frank, with XIX acting for Zilch.

A platform for European ambitions

Philip Belamant, CEO and co-founder at Zilch

The headquarters move sits alongside a cluster of strategic commitments that have changed the shape of the business this year. Zilch has announced the proposed acquisition of Fjord Bank, a deal that is expected to complete in the first half of 2027 and which the company says will form the foundation of its European expansion. It has also entered a multi-year strategic partnership with Visa and taken on a sponsorship arrangement as Arsenal FC’s official payments partner.

Cumulative customer spend on the Zilch platform has passed £8 billion across all UK regions, according to the company, and it counts six million customers on its books. Philip Belamant, co-founder and chief executive, said the new headquarters reflects “the scale of our ambition and the momentum behind our growth” and described the site as a base for attracting talent both domestically and internationally.

City Minister Lucy Rigby KC MP welcomed the announcement, describing the UK as “a fintech powerhouse” and voicing support for the sector’s continued growth.

Market and regulatory context

The Fjord Bank acquisition, once completed, would give Zilch a European banking licence and materially alter its regulatory footprint. For a BNPL provider that has operated largely under consumer-credit exemptions, holding a licensed deposit-taking entity in Europe carries both an opportunity and a compliance cost: greater product range and cross-border reach, but also capital requirements, prudential reporting obligations and exposure to the evolving Consumer Credit Directive framework across EU member states.

The broader BNPL sector has been navigating tightening oversight on both sides of the Channel. In the UK, the Treasury’s long-running consultation on bringing BNPL within the FCA regulatory perimeter has yet to conclude in final rules, though industry participants have been preparing for credit-authorisation requirements for several years. A banking licence acquired through Fjord Bank could allow Zilch to pre-empt some of that regulatory uncertainty by operating within an already-licenced structure.

Competitively, the move mirrors a pattern seen among better-capitalised BNPL players globally: consolidation upward into banking infrastructure rather than remaining as a merchant-facing credit layer. Klarna‘s pursuit of a public listing and Affirm’s continued push into debit and banking products reflect the same structural logic. Zilch’s Visa partnership adds an acceptance-network dimension that standalone BNPL products lack, potentially supporting the “intelligent payments platform” positioning the company has adopted as a framing that goes beyond instalment credit.

The Victoria headquarters lease is a long-duration fixed commitment, which signals confidence in the London talent market and the company’s trajectory. The proof of that conviction will come when the Fjord Bank deal closes and Zilch moves to convert the European banking licence into live product revenue.

title: PayPal Urges Retailers to Show BNPL Earlier as Black Friday Nears
snippet: PayPal research finds 67% of Christmas BNPL shoppers are more likely to add items to their basket when payment options appear on product pages. The post PayPal Urges Retailers to Show BNPL Earlier as Black Friday Nears appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
PayPal has published research ahead of the Black Friday and Cyber Monday peak, warning UK retailers that late disclosure of buy now, pay later options is costing them basket additions. The payments group says nine in ten UK adults are actively managing festive spending, and that visibility of instalment-payment options earlier in the shopping journey can materially shift conversion.

The research, conducted by Morning Consult on behalf of PayPal between 4 and 10 September 2026 among 2,076 UK adults, found that more than half of Christmas BNPL shoppers (55%) would favour a retailer that shows the option on product pages over one that waits until the checkout step, where only 21% said they preferred to see it. Two-thirds (67%) said earlier visibility would make them more likely to add an item to their basket. PayPal also cited its own internal data showing an 11% uplift in PayPal payment volumes among merchants that introduced Pay Later messaging or a second checkout button, though it noted results may vary and the underlying merchant sample dated from March 2020 to September 2025.

The BNPL placement argument

The distinction between product-page and checkout-page disclosure is commercially significant. At checkout, a shopper has already decided in principle to buy; instalment framing at that point reduces friction but does not drive discovery. On the product page, showing a weekly or monthly cost alongside a headline price addresses affordability earlier, when the shopper is still deciding whether to proceed. For higher-consideration purchases, that reframing can be the deciding factor.

UK home fitness retailer JTX Fitness offered a case study in the release. Jamie Forshaw, head of marketing at JTX Fitness, said: “Showing customers their payment options while they’re still browsing can help them feel more confident about how they’ll manage the cost. When customers can see Pay Later from the product page onwards, more of them go from browsing to buying.”

Sean Douglas, senior director of UK Large Enterprise at PayPal, noted that peak season pressure tends to put retailers in survival mode, but argued the data pointed to a more active opportunity: the 11% volume uplift, he said, could be the difference between meeting revenue targets and exceeding them.

Market context and regulatory backdrop

PayPal’s Pay Later sits within a BNPL market that is under active regulatory review in the UK. The Financial Conduct Authority has been developing a framework to bring point-of-sale credit products within the Consumer Credit Act perimeter, a process that has run for several years and is expected to introduce affordability check requirements, clearer pre-contract disclosure rules and new marketing standards. Once the regime is live, the question of where and how BNPL options are surfaced to consumers will move from a commercial optimisation decision to a compliance one.

The broader market for embedded BNPL includes Klarna, Clearpay (Afterpay) and Zilch, each of which also promotes early product-page integration to merchant partners. PayPal’s advantage in this space is distribution: its existing merchant acceptance network and buyer-side login reduce integration friction compared with a standalone BNPL provider. The research release is also a vehicle for directing merchants to PayPal’s Pay Later onboarding page, so the findings should be read in that commercial context.

The AI finding is a secondary data point worth watching. More than a third of respondents (35%) said they had used or planned to use AI for Christmas shopping, and 52% said they would use it specifically to find deals or compare prices. If AI-assisted browsing compresses the product discovery phase, the window in which payment messaging can influence a shopper may shift again, adding further complexity to where in the journey BNPL should appear.

FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: RemitBee and TerraPay Link Canadian SMEs to Digital Wallets
snippet: RemitBee has partnered with TerraPay to give Canadian small businesses access to cross-border payouts across 156 countries and 3.7 billion digital wallets. The post RemitBee and TerraPay Link Canadian SMEs to Digital Wallets appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
RemitBee, the Mississauga-based cross-border payments platform, has entered a partnership with London-headquartered TerraPay to extend international payout capabilities for Canadian small businesses and individual senders. The integration gives RemitBee’s customers access to TerraPay’s network, which spans 7.5 billion bank accounts and 3.7 billion digital wallets across more than 156 countries, with outbound corridors covering the United States, Asia, the Middle East and Africa.

The deal is framed around a specific gap in the Canadian market: small businesses have historically lacked the transaction volumes required to negotiate competitive exchange rates or access the kind of payment infrastructure available to larger corporates. RemitBee, which has been regulated by FINTRAC as a money services business since its founding in 2015, is positioning the partnership as a way to democratise enterprise-grade payment rails for SME use cases including supplier payments, freelancer payouts, remote payroll and remittances.

Manos Yoganathan, chief operating officer of RemitBee, said: “Canadian small and medium-sized businesses often lack the transaction volumes to negotiate favorable exchange rates and face delays in cross-border payments. By partnering with TerraPay, we’re advancing our vision of making enterprise-grade payment infrastructure accessible to these businesses.”

Market context

Canada’s outbound cross-border payments market is commercially significant. More than 90 per cent of employer businesses in the country are classified as small businesses, according to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada. That concentration of SMEs, combined with a diaspora population driving personal remittances, makes Canada an attractive corridor anchor for payments infrastructure providers. Global personal remittance flows to low- and middle-income countries reached approximately $704 billion in 2025, according to World Bank data cited in the release, a figure that illustrates the scale of the underlying demand.

TerraPay’s role in the partnership is to supply last-mile connectivity, particularly into digital wallets, a segment where traditional correspondent banking has the least reach. The company’s Xend network, which it describes as a wallet interoperability platform, is the mechanism through which those wallet payouts are routed. Several competing infrastructure providers, including Thunes and Nium, operate in broadly similar territory, offering single-connection access to multi-corridor payout networks for fintechs and payment operators. The competitive differentiation in this space tends to rest on the depth of wallet coverage in specific corridors, pricing transparency and the regulatory footprint of the infrastructure provider in receiving markets.

Regulatory path

Regulatory compliance is a stated priority for both parties. RemitBee’s FINTRAC registration covers its Canadian operations, and TerraPay emphasises its regulated status across multiple markets. Cross-border money movement into digital wallets is an area of active regulatory interest: the Financial Action Task Force has updated guidance on virtual asset service providers and wallet providers in recent years, and corridors into the Middle East and Africa carry additional compliance considerations given the concentration of mobile-money platforms operating under varied licensing regimes. For SME-facing operators, the ability to demonstrate clean compliance trails across corridors is becoming as commercially relevant as price.

The partnership does not include disclosed commercial terms or a go-live transaction volume target. The near-term markers to watch are the specific wallet networks activated within the TerraPay integration, uptake among RemitBee’s existing SME customer base, and whether the partnership extends into inbound Canadian corridors over time.

title: Visa and Mesh Partner to Bring Crypto Balances to 175m Merchants
snippet: The partnership lets consumers pay directly from crypto or stablecoin wallets at any Visa-accepting merchant, with no card pre-load required. The post Visa and Mesh Partner to Bring Crypto Balances to 175m Merchants appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Visa and Mesh have announced a strategic partnership designed to make crypto and stablecoin balances spendable across Visa’s global acceptance network of 175 million merchant locations in more than 200 countries. The deal targets what Mesh describes as the last-mile problem in digital-asset payments: the friction between owning crypto and actually spending it.

The mechanics are straightforward in principle. Mesh provisions a Visa credential behind the scenes when a consumer wants to pay. The user taps or checks out online as normal; the merchant receives a standard card payment with no new hardware or workflow changes required. Mesh handles the funding, conversion and, where required, KYC and user onboarding, acting as programme manager. The consumer does not need to pre-sell holdings, transfer funds to a bank account, or sign up for a separate card linked to a single platform.

The last-mile problem in context

The release cites Crypto.com research putting global crypto ownership at 774 million people as of June 2026. Yet American Banker data referenced in the release puts monthly crypto card volumes at roughly $1.5 billion by late 2025, a figure that, set against Visa’s $14.2 trillion in fiscal 2025 payment volume, illustrates how little of that ownership has converted into everyday spending. The gap is not primarily a product of consumer reluctance; it reflects the structural friction of existing rails. Every current route from a stablecoin balance to a fiat point-of-sale transaction requires a prior action by the consumer.

Mesh says it already serves more than 200 enterprise clients, including Kalshi, Tools for Humanity, Félix Pago, Majority and KAST, and its network connects hundreds of wallets, exchanges and platforms. That existing distribution is the commercial logic of the Visa deal: Visa brings ubiquitous merchant acceptance, and Mesh brings the orchestration layer that aggregates fragmented digital-asset balances.

“Crypto never had a spending problem, it has a last-mile problem, and until now, closing it meant getting a separate card,” said Bam Azizi, chief executive and co-founder of Mesh. “Mesh handles the funding and conversion, so a balance becomes purchasing power at the moment of payment, with nothing for the user to move and nothing for the merchant to change.”

Competitive and regulatory read-across

The partnership sits inside a broader push by card networks to integrate digital assets into traditional payment flows. Visa has previously worked with Circle and other stablecoin issuers on settlement rails, and Mastercard has pursued similar orchestration partnerships. The differentiator Mesh is positioning here is wallet-agnosticism: rather than tying the experience to a single issuer or platform, Mesh aggregates across wallets so a consumer can spend from whichever balance they hold, wherever they happen to be.

On the regulatory side, stablecoin payment infrastructure is drawing increasing legislative attention in both the US and the EU. In the US, the Genius Act and parallel House bills are progressing through Congress and would establish a federal licensing framework for stablecoin issuers, potentially clarifying the compliance path for programme managers like Mesh. In the EU, MiCA’s asset-referenced token provisions are already live, and the European Central Bank is watching stablecoin payment volumes with close interest. Neither development blocks the Visa-Mesh model, but both will shape how quickly participating platforms can onboard users in regulated jurisdictions.

The announcement does not confirm a launch date, name the first participating wallet platforms beyond existing Mesh clients, or disclose commercial terms. Rollout details are described as forthcoming. The key near-term markers are the jurisdictions where the product goes live first, the stablecoin denominations supported at launch, and whether any major consumer wallet outside Mesh’s existing enterprise roster signs on.

title: Dubai Future Finance Week day four: a tokenisation rulebook, a court on chain and the liquidity question
snippet: The DFSA published its view of how tokenised markets can scale and DIFC Courts proposed a way to enforce rulings on chain. On stage at the Future Tokenisation Forum, regulators and market builders agreed that issuing tokens is now the easy part. Making them tradeable is not. The post Dubai Future Finance Week day four: a tokenisation rulebook, a court on chain and the liquidity question appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The DFSA published its view of how tokenised markets can scale and DIFC Courts proposed a way to enforce rulings on chain. On stage at the Future Tokenisation Forum, regulators and market builders agreed that issuing tokens is now the easy part. Making them tradeable is not.

On Thursday, Dubai Future Finance Week turned to two longer-term questions: how family wealth passes between generations, and how tokenised assets can move from pilots into real markets. The Future Tokenisation Forum at Jumeirah Mina Al Salam took the second question, and it was the busiest regulatory day of the week.

A paper that maps the debate

Mark Steward, chief executive of the DFSA, opened the forum with the regulator’s new report, Scaling Tokenisation: The Road Ahead. It draws on input from BlackRock, Ripple, Robinhood, Soter Insure and Standard Chartered, and looks at what tokenisation needs as it moves from experiments into live financial products, payments and market infrastructure. The paper deliberately stops short of picking a winner. It sets out where the industry agrees and where it does not, and does not prescribe a particular technology, rulebook or business model. The DFSA wants it to start a wider conversation with firms, investors, policymakers and international standard setters.

DIFC Courts brought a more concrete proposal. Working with DECA4 Advisory and industry partners, the courts published a white paper on a Dispute Resolution Oracle, an opt-in link between a smart contract and a court or other forum the parties choose before they transact. The gap it targets is simple to state: a court can decide who owns a digital asset, but it cannot make that decision take effect on chain. Under the proposal, a disputed asset would be preserved once a claim is raised and the final decision enforced directly on chain. Judges, arbitrators and mediators would still decide cases off chain, with limited asset freezes, early review, reasoned decisions and rights of appeal as safeguards. The courts are pitching it as an open standard for any jurisdiction, not a Dubai-only tool. Amna Al Owais, deputy director of DIFC Courts, was among the day’s speakers.

Regulators: the wrapper changes, the rules should not

The regulators’ panel was the clearest guide to where supervisors stand. Michail Fekkas, first vice chairman of Greece’s Hellenic Capital Market Commission, argued that tokenisation changes how an instrument is issued, transferred and traded, not what it is. Europe already has the tools in MiFID, CSDR, the DLT Pilot Regime and MiCA, he said, and should not build a separate regime for tokenised assets. The principle should stay simple: same activity, same risk, same regulatory outcome. For him, the real obstacles are now legal uncertainty, fragmentation and whether market infrastructure can pay its way. “Europe must move from regulatory experimentation to regulatory scalability, and smaller European markets must be part of that,” he said.

William Mason, director general of the Guernsey Financial Services Commission, described a lighter-touch route. Guernsey audited its existing laws, found them largely fit for purpose and issued guidance on how it would read them, rather than rewriting them. He added that the GFSC aims to finalise its stablecoin rules next month. His bigger worry was liquidity. Supervisors do not want private assets moved on chain and sold to retail investors who then cannot get out, he said, and he doubted that automated market makers alone would solve it. Real market makers taking positions would be needed for the market to scale. “Buying is easy; anybody can buy,” he said. The hard part is being able to sell.

Paul Kayrouz, Chief Fintech Officer at the Central Bank of the UAE, gave the UAE’s position. The central bank regulates entities, he said, so a bank that starts tokenising securities needs a separate licence from the Capital Market Authority, but the central bank still oversees its whole balance sheet, operational resilience and conduct. On tokenised money, he said the UAE expects central bank digital currency, tokenised deposits and stablecoins to coexist rather than compete. The central bank’s job is to build the rails and let the market choose. The digital dirham is close to launch, the UAE has licensed four banks and one non-bank to issue stablecoins, and several banks are close to launching tokenised deposit programmes. To move beyond closed loops, he said, tokenised assets will need a unified ledger for clearing and settlement, and on-chain records with the same legal force as the assets they represent.

Kayrouz also pointed to a cross-border problem. A handful of stablecoin issuers dominate the market, and their tokens are used in the UAE although they are issued and licensed elsewhere. Protecting consumers then depends on regulators sharing information and working together, he said, because “we will never be in any stage where we will have the same regulation”. An Israeli regulator on the panel made a related point: owning a token used to be a technical question about who holds the key, but scaling it into finance needs a legal answer about enforceable rights, including across borders.

The market view: cheap to imagine, costly to issue

A second panel looked at why tokenisation has barely left the pilot stage. The founder of a UAE-based tokenisation platform said technology is no longer the bottleneck. Cost is: legal advice, issuing vehicles, licences and prospectuses mean the economics rarely work unless an issue runs into hundreds of millions of dollars. Today the money goes to lawyers, administrators and technology vendors, he said, and will shift towards distribution and trading as tokens trade across many venues. He expects funds and traditional capital markets to grow fastest, and warned that tokenising an asset with no clear use will fail. He also called the UAE lucky to have regulators that are approachable and willing to find ways to meet their objectives without blocking new products.

A speaker from the UAE’s Capital Market Authority, which replaced the SCA as a legal continuation on 1 January, said the authority’s tokenisation framework is still narrow, covering only securities and commodities. The CMA is considering a discussion paper to review it in light of market demand. Questions include which assets should qualify, how disclosure should work, who can custody tokens, and whether making illiquid assets easier to buy should change who they can be sold to. There is no single change that would unlock the market, she said.

Distribution: trust before scale

The forum’s closing panel, moderated by BCG, set the scale of the challenge: roughly USD 3trn in crypto assets and about USD 300bn in stablecoins, against only USD 30bn to 40bn in tokenised real-world assets. A partner at SC Ventures, Standard Chartered’s venture arm, said demand today comes mainly from crypto money looking for exposure to traditional assets. Institutions are next, once settlement and collateral benefits make the economics work, and everyone else will follow. Liquidity is the gap. “Just tokenising something doesn’t automatically make it liquid,” he said, adding that more market makers, leverage and links between traditional and digital rails would be needed.

Paul Boots, senior director and head of sector development at VARA, said the authority learns through regulatory pilots, including its expanding real estate tokenisation pilot with Dubai Land Department. Issuance rules are clear and licensed broker dealers can already distribute tokens. The next step is for tokens to trade on more than one platform with market makers behind them, so retail buyers of property tokens can sell when they need to. He was firm when an audience member asked VARA to make licensing easier: liquidity matters, but not at the expense of KYC and anti-money laundering checks. Investors, he said, will end up buying on “the platforms of trust”.

Mohamed Damak, managing director and global head of Islamic finance at S&P Global Ratings, said S&P has rated some tokenised money market funds and digital bonds at the same level as their conventional equivalents after finding that the technology added no extra risk. He named three barriers to scale: the legal structure of what a token holder owns, interoperability between bank platforms and public blockchains, and the money leg, where settlement still waits for banks to open. He pointed to the DIFC Courts proposal as the kind of recourse investors will want before they commit. The president of Robinhood MENA, which arrived in the UAE recently, said investor education remains the biggest hurdle for retail demand.

Family wealth and the next generation

The Dubai Family Wealth Summit, held the same day, focused on governance, succession, structuring and philanthropy, with the UAE’s Year of Family as the backdrop. Dr Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, Minister of Foreign Trade, gave the keynote on international connectivity. Speakers included Hussain Sajwani of DAMAC, Halima Dangote of Dangote Industries, Maurice Gravier of Emirates NBD, Shehab Gargash of Gargash Prime and Osama Ibrahim Seddiqi of Seddiqi Holding. DIFC announced a 2027 NextGen Internship Programme that will place future family business leaders in DIFC firms across financial services, audit, consultancy, law and AI, Fintech and innovation, ahead of an estimated USD 18.3trn global wealth transfer by 2030. The Investment Leaders Exchange brought sovereign wealth funds, institutional allocators and family offices together on asset allocation and the place of digital assets in long-term portfolios.

Dr Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, Minister of Foreign Trade

A China to Gulf payments link

Outside the forums, Lianlian DigiTech, the Hong Kong-listed payments group, opened its Middle East regional office in DIFC. The company already holds a DFSA Category 3D payment services licence and will offer cross-border collections, foreign exchange and vendor payouts for businesses trading between China, the Gulf and global markets. It already supports sellers on Noon, Amazon UAE and Amazon Saudi Arabia.

Dubai Future Finance Week closes on Friday with GEFI’s ethical finance conference at DIFC.

title: COLIBRIX ONE Taps Vivox AI for Automated KYB Merchant Onboarding
snippet: The FCA- and MFSA-authorised payments platform will use Vivox AI's explainable agents to verify corporate documents and run sanctions screening on new merchants. The post COLIBRIX ONE Taps Vivox AI for Automated KYB Merchant Onboarding appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
COLIBRIX ONE, the payments infrastructure platform operated within the Mellifera group, has selected Vivox AI under a multi-year agreement to automate know-your-business checks across its UK and EU merchant base. The deal is designed to reduce the time compliance analysts spend processing document-heavy due diligence on new business customers without removing human sign-off from the process.

Under the arrangement, Vivox AI’s explainable AI agents will handle corporate document verification, ultimate beneficial owner mapping, and sanctions and adverse media screening. Every AI-generated finding is traceable to its underlying source, and COLIBRIX ONE’s compliance team will review and approve each case before it is closed. The rollout covers merchant onboarding in the UK and EU, with plans to extend to ongoing monitoring and additional entity types in 2027.

What the technology does

Vivox AI’s agents draw on corporate registry data across more than 155 countries to identify ownership structures, shareholders and directors, then generate a full customer due diligence or enhanced due diligence report for analyst review. In an earlier deployment at international payments firm TransferMate, the company said due diligence time fell from roughly 60 minutes to under 15 minutes per case, with screening alerts declining by 86 per cent. Those figures come from Vivox AI’s own account of the TransferMate project and have not been independently verified.

Tim Khamzin, founder and chief executive of Vivox AI, said: “AI agents take on the document-heavy due diligence work where every conclusion comes with a clear audit trail, so analysts stay in control and regulators can see exactly how a decision was reached. That is what makes AI usable in a regulated business.”

COLIBRIX ONE is authorised by the UK Financial Conduct Authority as an electronic money institution (FRN 927920) and holds a parallel authorisation through Mellifera Kartiera Limited from the Malta Financial Services Authority. Its product stack includes card acquiring for one-time and recurring transactions, multi-currency current accounts with dedicated named IBANs, and global payouts, with principal memberships at Visa and Mastercard.

Regulatory and market context

The timing reflects a specific pressure on payment platforms regulated under UK and EU financial crime frameworks. The FCA has tightened its expectations on anti-money laundering controls and merchant due diligence for e-money institutions in recent years, and the EU’s AML package, including the forthcoming AML Authority, will raise baseline obligations further across the bloc. For platforms that compete partly on onboarding speed, manual KYB on merchants with complex, multi-jurisdiction ownership structures is a genuine operational bottleneck.

The market for AI-assisted compliance tooling is expanding quickly. Established regtech vendors and a new generation of AI-native compliance firms are competing to automate the same document-heavy workflows, often positioning explainability and audit-trail quality as the differentiator that makes their products acceptable to risk functions and supervisors alike. COLIBRIX ONE’s choice of a dedicated AI compliance vendor rather than a bundled solution from its existing technology stack reflects a broader pattern among licensed payment firms: separating the compliance workflow layer from the core processing infrastructure in order to swap components as the tooling matures.

The key variable to watch in deployments like this one is whether the efficiency gains cited from the TransferMate reference hold across a larger and more varied merchant portfolio, particularly for merchants with layered holding structures in higher-risk jurisdictions, where beneficial ownership mapping is hardest and regulatory tolerance for errors is lowest.

fullText:
Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

You can find more information:

NCSC, Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography 

G7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sector 

CMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

title: Emirates NBD and BlackRock Launch Two Funds at Partnership Anniversary
snippet: The one-year-old collaboration has gathered $350m in AUM and now expands into CLO and systematic income strategies for retail wealth clients. The post Emirates NBD and BlackRock Launch Two Funds at Partnership Anniversary appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Emirates NBD Asset Management and BlackRock have launched two income-focused public funds to mark the first anniversary of their strategic partnership, broadening a collaboration that began in 2025 with access to private market alternatives and has since accumulated $350 million in assets under management.

The two new products are the FundStar Emirates CLO AA Fund, sub-managed by BlackRock, and the Emirates Systematic Income and Growth Fund, for which BlackRock serves as investment adviser while Emirates NBD Asset Management retains portfolio management responsibility. Both are now available to the bank’s retail and wealth clients across the region.

The funds in detail

The CLO fund invests in a portfolio of senior secured corporate loans across the US and Europe, targeting an average credit rating of AA with no sub-investment-grade exposure. It offers daily liquidity and carries no leverage, positioning it as a relatively conservative floating-rate income vehicle. BlackRock’s CLO franchise spans more than 24 years and manages over $40 billion globally in the strategy, which lends the product credible institutional provenance.

The Systematic Income and Growth Fund takes a benchmark-unconstrained approach, allocating across globally diversified income-producing assets using BlackRock’s systematic investment models. It targets a net distribution rate of 7% per annum, paid quarterly. That headline yield will attract scrutiny from wealth advisers assessing whether the return compensates adequately for the underlying complexity and variability of a multi-asset systematic strategy.

Michail Samawi, senior executive officer at Emirates NBD Asset Management, described the launch as fulfilling a commitment to “democratise premium global investments” for Middle East wealth clients. Keith Saldanha, BlackRock’s head of wealth and global product solutions for the Middle East and Africa, said the partnership demonstrated “significant opportunity for both CLO and systematic strategies within wealth portfolios.”

Market context and regulatory read-across

The move from private-market-only structures aimed at professional clients to public funds accessible to retail investors is a material step. Retail-eligible fund structures in the UAE fall under the oversight of the Securities and Commodities Authority, which has tightened disclosure and suitability requirements for complex products in recent years. The transition signals Emirates NBD Asset Management’s confidence that its distribution infrastructure and compliance framework can support a broader investor base, but it also raises the bar for product documentation and ongoing suitability assessment.

The CLO market itself has attracted renewed institutional interest across the Gulf, as dollar-denominated floating-rate products offer a natural hedge against rate uncertainty that regional investors with dollar-pegged liabilities value. Several global asset managers, including but not limited to BlackRock, have sought to package CLO exposure into fund wrappers accessible below institutional minimums, responding to strong private banking demand in Dubai and Riyadh.

The partnership model here, where a regional bank provides distribution and local regulatory relationships while a global manager provides investment capability, is becoming a standard template across the Gulf Cooperation Council. Similar structures have emerged between regional banks and global alternatives managers in Saudi Arabia under the Capital Market Authority‘s push to deepen local capital markets. The competitive question for Emirates NBD Asset Management is how quickly it can grow AUM in the new public funds relative to the $350 million gathered in the first year, and whether the 7% distribution target on the systematic fund holds across a full market cycle.

snippet: The bank aims to expand its reach to more customers by offering services via the NCR Atleos ATMs in Target stores.

        Published Nov. 6, 2026

Dive Brief:

First Citizens Bank is partnering with NCR Atleos to offer surcharge-free access to services via ATMs located at some 2,000 Target stores, the bank said in a press release last month. As part of the agreement, the bank’s customers can use the ATMs at Target stores to withdraw cash, check their account balances and transfer funds to eligible linked accounts without paying a fee, according to the Oct. 19 release.

“The consumer banking experience needs to meet customers where they are through multiple channels, whether in-person or digitally enabled,” First Citizens Bank’s head of consumer banking, Michael Wilson, said in the release. 

Meanwhile, NCR Atleos CEO Tim Oliver said Wednesday that the company’s sale to Brink’s is progressing, with expected completion of the transaction by January.

Dive Insight:

For NCR Atleos, which became a standalone company three years ago, the partnership with First Citizens allows it to add new service providers to its roster. 

The company separated from its parent in late 2023, creating two publicly traded companies: NCR Voyix and NCR Atleos. While NCR Atleos offers ATMs and other interactive teller machines for payments and banking services, NCR Voyix offers point-of-sale hardware and related services to restaurant, retail and other merchants.

As NCR Atleos has grown its corporate clientele, including by working with American Express and PayNearMe in recent years, its self-service banking segment has bolstered revenue. The company reported third-quarter earnings results Wednesday that showed its self-service banking segment rose 3% to $2.17 billion for the first nine months of the year, faster than its overall business revenue growth, which increased 2% to $3.23 billion for the period, according to the earnings press release. 

“Our service-led growth initiatives and investment in product innovation are encouraging financial institutions and retailers to choose our differentiated and comprehensive offering to meet their evolving self-service needs,” Oliver said in August when the company reported second-quarter earnings. 

NCR’s partnership with First Citizens comes as the ATM provider prepares to be acquired. In February, the Brink’s Company agreed to buy NCR Atleos in a cash and stock transaction valued at about $6.6 billion. As part of the deal, Brink’s will also take on $2.6 billion in NCR Atleos debt, a press release on the transaction said. 

Regulators have yet to approve the deal. The Competition and Markets Authority in the U.K. said Brink’s acquisition of NCR Atleos could limit competition, according to a September report from the news outlet Reuters. Earlier this month, the Wall Street Journal reported Brink’s plans to sell some subsidiaries in a move aimed at assuaging U.K. concerns.

“We continue to make meaningful progress on regulatory approval processes across the multiple jurisdictions, and have significantly advanced the integration planning activities for the pending combination of Atleos and The Brink’s Company,” Oliver said in the release this week.

title: In Profile: Sid Powell, CEO and Co-Founder at Maple Finance
snippet: Maple Finance chief executive Sid Powell on bringing securitisation onchain, why DeFi is judged by its worst week, and winning over institutional allocators. The post In Profile: Sid Powell, CEO and Co-Founder at Maple Finance appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Sid Powell spent his early career inside the plumbing of traditional credit markets, working on securitisation, corporate finance and credit risk at National Australia Bank before becoming portfolio manager and treasurer at an Australian non-bank lender.

Sid Powell, CEO and co-founder at Maple Finance

In 2019 he co-founded Maple Finance, an onchain asset manager that builds institutional credit infrastructure on public blockchains. The firm says it has originated more than $24 billion in loans and now manages more than $4.6 billion in assets.

In this In Profile, Sid Powell, CEO and co-founder at Maple Finance, discusses bringing securitisation onchain, why DeFi is judged by its worst week, and what it will take for institutional allocators to follow.

Tell us more about your company and its purpose

Maple is an onchain asset manager, meaning we’re a platform that uses blockchain infrastructure to manage both crypto and traditional assets. We build institutional grade credit infrastructure on public blockchains, pairing traditional capital markets fundamentals with the transparency and settlement speed crypto rails make possible. We started in 2019 on the idea that credit markets don’t need to be opaque in order to be safe. Every loan we originate sits on a public transparency page, so lenders can see collateralisation and performance in real time instead of waiting on a quarterly report.

Since 2022 we’ve originated more than $24 billion in loans across multiple market cycles, spanning secured lending and structured credit for institutional borrowers and lenders. More recently, we’ve built products like syrupUSDC and syrupUSDG that bring that same institutional grade yield to a much wider audience, including people on mainstream platforms who never touch decentralised finance (DeFi) directly. The purpose hasn’t changed since day one: make credit markets more transparent and more efficient, without cutting corners on risk.

What are some of your recent achievements you’d like to highlight?

An achievement I’m proudest of this year is launching our own token, syrupUSDG, with Robinhood and Paxos. It went live on Ethereum and on Robinhood Chain at the same time, so retail users had access to institutional-grade onchain yield immediately. It’s our first new syrup product in two years and the clearest signal yet that mainstream fintech is treating onchain infrastructure as credible rather than experimental. To demonstrate the scale, Robinhood alone reported 28.4 million funded customers and $369 billion in platform assets last quarter, and the Global Dollar Network that syrupUSDG plugs into has grown past $3.5 billion in circulation across more than 150 enterprise partners.

We also launched the Kraken Warehouse structure in June, a real, working case study in how DeFi capital gets put to productive economic use. I was particularly proud of this because I came from a securitisation banking background, and one of the original dreams for Maple was to bring securitisation onchain.

And finally, another proud achievement was Fortune naming Maple to its 2026 Crypto Innovators list, which meant a lot for our team.

How did you get into the fintech industry?

After years in traditional finance, I saw first-hand how slow lending can be. At National Australia Bank, I worked across securitisation, corporate finance and credit risk, then as portfolio manager and treasurer at Angle Finance, a non-bank lender funding small and medium businesses across Australia.

Both roles put me inside the plumbing of credit markets: structuring deals, managing risk, and watching how long it takes to verify collateral or settle a facility when everything runs through intermediaries and manual processes. I was looking for the next technology shift in finance and as I started learning more about blockchain and smart contracts, I could see that this would be a major platform shift which would enable new winners to emerge. This presented an exciting opportunity to try and build one of those winners. So co-founding Maple was a chance to build the credit market I wished I’d had on the other side of those deals: transparent, faster to settle, and just as disciplined about risk.

What’s the best thing about working in the fintech industry?

The best thing about working in fintech is watching formerly slow processes happen in real time. In traditional credit, verifying collateral, confirming a loan is performing, and settling a transaction can each take days. But on blockchain, that same information is visible instantly to anyone who wants to check it. That shift, from “trust me” to see-for-yourself, is what got me excited about this space, and it’s still what excites me most about it now. The other part is the pace of convergence. A few years ago, a bank or a brokerage building on public blockchain rails was a novelty. Now it’s a live product decision inside firms managing large volumes of real customer money. Being close to that shift, and building some of the infrastructure it runs on, is a front-row seat into the future of finance.

What frustrates you most about the fintech industry?

The industry still gets judged by its worst week. April was a rough month for DeFi broadly, with security incidents at other protocols driving real losses, and it coloured how a lot of people talked about the whole space for weeks afterwards. That’s a fair thing for outsiders to be cautious about. What’s frustrating is when caution turns into “this is all the same thing,” when in reality risk management, transparency and underwriting standards vary enormously from one platform to the next. We built our business on being the more conservative, mature and transparent option, and it’s frustrating when that distinction gets flattened in the coverage.

How have your previous roles influenced your career?

My background shaped how I operate now and I owe a lot to the mentors I had during my time in banking. Securitisation at NAB taught me a lot of fundamentals about structuring deals, analysing cash flows and downside protection. It’s fundamentally about breaking assets into cash flows and understanding exactly what’s backing a set of obligations, which isn’t far from how we think about structuring loans and collateral at Maple; it’s just moved onchain. Credit risk work forces a certain discipline, ensuring you don’t get comfortable with an exposure just because it hasn’t gone wrong yet. That instinct shaped how conservative we’ve tried to be about risk management and transparency at Maple.

My work in treasury and portfolio management, including managing funding, liquidity and a live book of loans to small businesses, is the piece that translates most directly to running Maple day to day. We balance growth against risk, and never assume a portfolio performing today will keep performing without active management. I don’t think I’d run this business the same way without having sat on both sides of that table first.

What’s the best mistake you’ve ever made?

The most useful mistake we’ve made was mistaking optionality for progress. Early on, we tried to advance too many initiatives at once. It felt ambitious, but it diluted focus and slowed execution. The lesson was that conviction only matters if it is concentrated. Since then, we’ve run Maple around fewer, higher-conviction priorities, with clear ownership and a much higher bar for taking on anything new. We don’t spend much time regretting mistakes. We extract the lesson, change the system, and move on.

What has the future got in store for your company?

At Maple, we’re excited about what’s ahead. Expect to see more of the fintech distribution model we proved out with Robinhood, and more institutions bringing real credit structures onchain the way we’re doing with our current facilities. I already said publicly that “every fintech will offer yield on stablecoin balances within the next two years.” Maple will become the credit manager behind most of that yield. On the institutional side, we expect to keep seeing traditional finance players move real credit structures onchain. That powerful shift towards onchain credit will soon simply be how a deal gets done. Maple is pioneering the future of onchain asset management, one deal at a time.

What are the next key talking points or challenges for your industry as a whole?

Regulatory clarity is the big challenge for DeFi. Guidance on how stablecoins get classified has become very real this year, and you can see the effect directly, with firms like Robinhood and Tempo shipping products that would have been hard to justify building eighteen months ago. The next challenge is proving that clarity was worth waiting for.

The next big bridge for the industry to cross is how we get institutional allocators to start deploying onchain. This is what will drive the next order of magnitude of growth. In a lot of ways, the blockchain space is still reliant on early adopters among retail and high net worth. Bitcoin ETFs, vaults and tokenised stocks are helping to familiarise institutional investors but as of yet, examples of them allocating onchain are isolated and rare.

The other conversation the industry needs to keep having, honestly, is about risk management standards. This year’s DeFi hacks showed that not every protocol manages collateral and underwriting in the same way, and the ones that do it well need to be louder about how, not just that they didn’t get hit. Transparency has to be a selling point the industry competes on, to help it build the trust it deserves.

title: FIS, Toast CFOs exit
snippet: The chief financial officers are leaving the payments players as the companies grapple with separate challenges.
fullText:
Fidelity National Information Services and Toast separately disclosed that their chief financial officers are exiting, as they also announced third-quarter earnings results. 

At FIS, which provides payments services to banking and capital markets clients, the company announced the departure of James Kehoe, with no further explanation. Alexandra “Alex” Brooks will step into the CFO post on an interim basis starting Thursday as the company begins a search for a permanent replacement, according to a Wednesday press release.

The CFO change at Jacksonville, Florida-based FIS landed as the company adjusted its financial forecasts due to unexpected changes in the outlook for recurring revenue, citing new factors that are dragging on that income.

The shifts were mainly related to changed expectations at some of its banking clients as those customers encounter implementation delays and, in some cases, work through acquisition activity, CEO Stephanie Ferris explained on a webcast with analysts Wednesday. The change is happening as some customers move from services with more traditional licenses to the company’s more updated subscription software services, she said.

“Over the course of the third quarter, we started to see some client-directed conversion delays, primarily in our larger client base, and some impacts from the timing around large bank consolidation,” Ferris said on the webcast.

FIS divests prepaid business

She also noted that the company would invest in technology and security to assist clients with implementations and to prioritize cyber work.

“These factors will weigh on our results in the fourth quarter in 2027, and we expect them to largely fade in 2028,” Ferris said. 

FIS also disclosed during the third-quarter report that it had sold what it referred to as a “non-core, prepaid asset” for $100 million. A spokesperson for the company didn’t immediately respond to requests for more information about the unit or the buyer.

Kehoe has been with FIS since August 2023, joining shortly after Ferris became CEO in January of that year. Together, they took the company through a $24.25 billion sale last year of its merchants services business Worldpay to Global Payments, and the $13.5 billion acquisition of a card issuer business from Global Payments.

FIS reported third-quarter adjusted net earnings rose 5.3% to $831 million as operating revenue climbed 29%, on an adjusted basis, to $3.37 billion, according to the company’s earnings press release.

At Toast, the digital payments processor said that its president and chief financial officer, Elena Gomez, will leave her posts at the end of the year. Michael Senno, who has served as Toast’s senior vice president of finance, will become CFO at that time, the company said.

Gomez, who has been at Toast since May 2021 and guided the company through its initial public offering that year, said in the company’s earnings press release that it’s time “to take a break before my next chapter.”

Toast CEO criticizes lawsuit

Meanwhile, during a webcast with analysts on Tuesday, Toast’s CEO, Aman Narang, continued to make a case for fighting a lawsuit brought by the Federal Trade Commission and states last week. The federal and state regulators alleged in their lawsuit that the company exacted “hidden fees” and “unauthorized charges” from both merchants and consumers. 

Narang defended the contracts Toast negotiates with every restaurant, and other merchants, to provide services in the business-to-business industry. 

The lawsuit turns on the Federal Trade Commission Act and the Restore Online Shoppers’ Confidence Act, barring companies from misleading customers. The regulators said Toast made “false or misleading claims” regarding its subscription and financing services; failed to make required disclosures; didn’t provide simple ways for customers to cancel their subscription; and charged customers without their consent. 

“We are incredibly disappointed with the FTC's decision to file the suit,” Narang told analysts on the earnings webcast. “We've been engaged with them and cooperating with them really over the past year, and fundamentally believe their application of ROSCA is unprecedented for custom contracts in B2B.”

Narang posited that the enforcement action on that basis could impact the entire industry. “If ROSCA were to apply to B2B custom negotiated contracts in a B2B context, it would have huge implications for, really, the whole industry and business contracts in general,” Narang contended. “We have a lot of confidence in our business practices and are ready to defend ourselves.”

Dive Brief:

Payment processor Riverside Payments, its affiliate Cascade Equipment Leasing LLC and their operators have agreed to pay $600,000 to settle allegations that they deceived small businesses about payment-processing costs and cancellation terms, the Federal Trade Commission said Monday.

The proposed settlement, which stems from a joint action with Washington state, also allows affected small businesses to terminate their payment-processing agreements without an early termination penalty, the FTC said.

“Riverside and Cascade promised small businesses significant savings, but instead of saving money locked them into costly, multi-year contracts and made it very difficult to cancel,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a press release. “The FTC will hold accountable companies that deceive small businesses, whose hard work powers our economy.”

Dive Insight:

The FTC and Washington alleged in their complaint that Riverside promised businesses they could save 40% to 60% by switching payment processors. In reality, businesses that switched typically ended up paying more than they had with their previous providers, according to the complaint, which was filed Monday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington, along with a proposed order resolving the charges.

The companies allegedly failed to disclose several fees in sales quotes, including activation fees, batch fees and charges related to data security compliance or inactive processing, the government alleged. Riverside also allegedly buried important contract terms in a 26-page electronic agreement.

Those terms included automatic renewal of payment-processing services after an initial three-year contract, a $695 early termination fee and equipment leases through Cascade that extended one year beyond the processing agreement, according to the complaint.

The FTC and Washington also allege Riverside advertised a “no-risk” cancellation guarantee, promising customers they could cancel at any time without penalty, switch back to their previous processor and receive $500 for their time and trouble. Businesses seeking to leave instead allegedly faced repeated phone calls and delays, with some never receiving promised callbacks.

The complaint also challenges Riverside's earnings claims to prospective sales agents. The company advertised that agents could earn $75,000 to $95,000 annually, with top performers making $100,000. In reality, agents earned an average of $3,787 per year, according to the complaint.

The proposed order imposes a $32.1 million judgment against Riverside, Cascade and their owners, Brandon Skinner and Jason Reese. The judgment will be suspended after the defendants pay $600,000 because of their alleged inability to pay the full amount, the FTC said. The full judgment would be due if they are found to have misrepresented their financial circumstances, the agency said in its press release.

The order also requires the defendants to notify customers that they can terminate their merchant-processing agreements without paying early termination fees or other penalties during a 60-day period.

Under the proposed order, the companies would be prohibited from misrepresenting service costs, potential savings and cancellation terms. They would also have to disclose material contract terms before collecting billing information, obtain customers' express informed consent for recurring billing arrangements and provide a straightforward cancellation process.

The companies could not be reached for comment.

title: Debenhams Group Embeds Storfund Daily Advance for 30,000 Sellers
snippet: Debenhams Group has partnered with Storfund to give marketplace sellers up to 80% of shipped-order revenue daily, ahead of peak Christmas trading. The post Debenhams Group Embeds Storfund Daily Advance for 30,000 Sellers appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Debenhams Group has embedded Storfund‘s Daily Advance product directly into its marketplace platform, giving more than 30,000 brand partners access to up to 80% of their shipped-order revenue on a daily basis rather than waiting for the standard settlement cycle. The service went live in October 2026, timed ahead of the Christmas peak trading window.

Dan Finley, Group CEO at Debenhams Group

Under the arrangement, Storfund advances the 80% share each day as orders are dispatched. When Debenhams Group makes its scheduled marketplace payment to a partner, the funds flow into a Storfund-nominated account, at which point Storfund releases the remaining 20% to the seller, net of applicable fees. Participation is optional, subject to Storfund eligibility criteria, and carries no subscription, set-up fee or minimum term. Eligible sellers can use the service across Debenhams, boohoo and PrettyLittleThing without additional administration.

Dan Finley, chief executive of Debenhams Group, said the move was designed to make Debenhams Group the preferred platform for brands seeking to scale: “Giving sellers faster access to their sales revenue gives them greater flexibility to reinvest in their businesses when they need it most, particularly as we head into peak Christmas trading.”

The marketplace liquidity play

The launch is a structural extension of Debenhams Group’s broader pivot towards a marketplace model. Marketplace now accounts for 38.9% of the group’s gross merchandise value, up from 32.7% in the comparable period a year earlier, a shift that positions the group closer to a platform operator than a traditional retailer. Faster seller liquidity is a lever that platform operators use to attract and retain supply: when sellers can recycle working capital quickly, they hold deeper stock, respond faster to demand signals and are less likely to de-prioritise a platform in favour of a competitor with quicker settlement.

Storfund positions itself as a liquidity layer for marketplace sellers globally, with existing integrations on Amazon, TikTok Shop and Booking.com. Justin Hanna, the company’s director of platform partnerships, framed the Debenhams integration as part of a broader market trajectory: “Marketplaces have spent the last decade building better shopping, advertising, fulfilment and settlement experiences. Liquidity is the next frontier.”

Market context and competitive read-across

Marketplace seller financing is an increasingly contested segment. Amazon operates its own Lending programme for third-party sellers, while several specialist working-capital providers, including Payoneer, Clearco and Uncapped, compete for the same cohort of e-commerce businesses. The distinguishing feature of an embedded model, where the advance product sits inside the marketplace rather than requiring a seller to seek out a standalone lender, is friction reduction: eligibility can be tied to platform data rather than traditional credit underwriting.

From a regulatory standpoint, the product as described resembles a revenue-based advance or purchase-of-receivables arrangement rather than a consumer credit facility, which typically places it outside the FCA‘s consumer credit regime. However, if Storfund’s eligibility and fee structures are applied to smaller sole-trader sellers, the regulatory perimeter warrants monitoring as the FCA continues to refine its approach to buy-now-pay-later and alternative credit instruments.

The forward indicators to watch are the take-up rate among Debenhams Group’s seller base, whether Storfund extends the integration to the full set of group marketplaces beyond the three named at launch, and any update on fee economics that would allow an independent assessment of the cost of capital for sellers using the service.
